title: M82 (NIRCam image - shorter wavelengths)
caption: The center of the starburst galaxy M82, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: M82 · constellation Ursa Major · about 12 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, A. Bolatto (UMD)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Webb press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A bright white core glows against the blackness of space, with dark brown tendrils of dust packed toward the center. White points of many sizes are scattered across the scene, crowding most thickly near the middle. This is a section of M82, an edge-on starburst galaxy, seen in near-infrared light by Webb.

Found in Ursa Major, M82 is 12 million light-years from Earth. It is forming stars 10 times faster than the Milky Way. For a long time, curtains of dust and gas have hidden that process from view, but Webb's infrared vision can see through them.

With Webb's sharp resolution, astronomers can pick out small, bright, compact sources, each of which is either a single star or a star cluster. An accurate tally of them could reveal the separate stages of star birth and how long each stage takes.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (0.76 x 0.76 arcminutes) and distance (12 million light years), the frame spans roughly 2,700 × 2,700 light-years. Its light set out about 12 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Webb's Near-Infrared Camera, NIRCam. Red shows light at 2.12 microns, green at 1.64 microns and blue at 1.40 microns.
understand.eye: All of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye. In visible light, the dust that Webb sees through would hide much of this detail.

explore: The NIRCam view shows the galaxy's center in unprecedented detail. It comes from a survey of M82 by a team of astronomers using Webb. Webb's infrared view makes such a census possible.
alt: A bright white galactic core with dark brown dust tendrils and many white points of stars and clusters concentrated toward the center.
